The current version of the lift tactic makes use of CanLift instances, in which the condition (argument cond) is an outParam. This is because when the tactic is called on a : A with lift a to B using foo, the type of foo is not known, or at least has metavariables (or, even worse, using is optional, so there is no term for which we can check the type!). Consequently, the tactic performs a type class search on the type A of a, and B looking for a CanLift A B ?_ ?_ instance. Upon finding one, it infers the coe and cond fields and checks that foo : cond a.

This is suboptimal, because it means we can only ever supply one kind of condition to lift one type to another. In certain cases, like lifting ℤ to ℕ, that's fine because there is really only one condition that makes sense: 0 ≤ n. But for others, there may be a plethora of options. For example, when lifting z : ℂ to ℝ, possible valid conditions include z.im = 0, star z = z, z = ↑z.re, ‖z‖ = ‖z.re‖, and many more besides. In the current setup, we can only ever supply a proof that z.im = 0. As another example, to lift a LinearMap to a ContinuousLinearMap, one may wish to supply a proof of continuity, but currently, unless the domain is finite dimensional, this fails because the CanLift instance assumes the space is finite dimensional and the condition is cond := fun _ ↦ True. The problem is exacerbated when one wants to, e.g, lift an indexed family of linear maps to an indexed family of continuous linear maps. This should be possible (since there is a CanLift instance for pi types), but this would again fail unless the domain of each of these in finite dimensional.

I would like to overcome this problem in the following way.

  1. Make the cond field of CanLift a semiOutParam (I guess we could also make coe a semiOutParam, but that's maybe a bit more strange).
  2. When performing type class synthesis, return the coercion and an Array of conditions.
  3. If using foo is supplied, check if foo : cond _ for any cond in the array. If any succeeds, proceed, if not, fail.
  4. If using is not supplied, look for a default_instance of CanLift A B _ ?cond, and return a goal of ?cond _ as the tactic currently does. If no default_instance is found, complain.

One downside: this could cause some amount of combinatorial explosion when used in conjunction with the parametric CanLift instances (like docs#CanLift, docs#Prod.instCanLift), especially if multiple instances of these are added. However, I think there is little reason to do so, and I think that in practice, the combinatorial explosion will likely not be too large. One alternative would be to have two CanLift classes, one of which allows the cond to vary and the other doesn't, which would allow you to reduce the search space. But I think this is trying to solve a problem that may not exist in practice.

cc: @Bhavik Mehta and @Rob Lewis with whom I discussed this briefly at ICERM.

:thinking: I think instead maybe picking the cond for non-using goals should be done via priority instead of default_instance because the latter will return all CanLift _ _ _ _ which we then have to filter only to CanLift A B _ _.

Your proposal of returning an array of conditions is not possible with type class search, because type class search only ever gives you one result.

What I think is possible though, is:

  1. If the type of cond is fully known (doesn't contain any metavariables), then run type class search in order to find a CanLift instance where cond is exactly this value
  2. If the type of cond is not fully known, use the current behaviour, so infer the value of cond in type class search. Which one is synthesized depends on the priorities of the available instances.

Do you think this is sufficient for what you want?

In examples like this, should we add a new predicate Complex.isReal that has a whole lot of different constructors, like Complex.isReal.of_im_eq_zero and .of_star_eq_self etc...
We could then possibly tag those constructors with some attribute, and the CanLift tactic could try those constructors against foo (if there is a using foo clause) or against local hyps.
I think docs#IsSelfAdjoint is that predicate
I'm thinking more of the general pattern, together with the attribute system. Maybe I should have made that more clear.

@Jovan Gerbscheid it's not terribly hard to handroll this. I talked about it with Thomas Murrills on Friday, and, because there are not very many parametric CanLift instances, you don't return a ridiculous number of results. Essentially, you can use docs#Lean.Elab.SynthInstance.getInstance to find the top-level instances that apply, and then synthesize the instance arguments of those, using the standard method for most, but recursively calling this function when the argument is another CanLift instance.

@Johan Commelin yes, I also considered the bespoke predicate design, but I hoped to avoid it if possible. It would be pretty annoying to have a LinearMap.IsContinuous predicate just for the purposes of lift.
But Continuous is already this predicate?
I find it weird to complexify the lift tactic to avoid using a lemma translating to the normal form of a condition

The whole point of the current CanLift instance for linear maps is that you don't have to think about it, the lift just works automatically without supplying any proof. I think that's great, but if we make Continuous the only option, then we have to supply the proof again.

Okay, I will make a different attempt here and report back with an alternative suggestion.

So, I've thought about this a bit more and I want to highlight something that maybe wasn't clear in what I was saying above. Before we begin, note that we should have the following instance (mainly for use with the existing docs#Prod.instCantLift), regardless of our other decisions:

/-- Useful in conjunction with `Prod.instCanLift` to lift only one element in a pair. -/
instance instCanLiftId (α : Sort*) : CanLift α α (fun x ↦ x) (fun _ ↦ True) where
  prf a _ := ⟨a, rfl⟩

A key advantage of the typeclass based approach is that, by doing the recursion, you can get all the possible conditions, and potentially return them to the user to select from with a lift? a to B variant which outputs something like lift a to B using (?_ : condition chosen by user). I think that this is not so easy to do in general if you use the single predicate approach in the presence of parametric CanLift instances (i.e., those that take a CanLift instance as an argument). The issue is that the prediate for lifting α × β to γ × δ is just docs#And. So to lift ℕ × ℂ to ℕ × ℝ, the predicate would be fun x ↦ True ∧ Complex.IsReal x.2. But if we want to split that Complex.IsReal into a bunch of options using various @[lift] tagged lemmas, then we need to somehow deconstruct this predicate, remembering which pieces of it came from CanLift conditions, and finding all the options associated to those. This seems very hard to me unless we create a bespoke predicate for every kind of lift (in which case we could perform the deconstruction on the head symbol), but this would mean adding synonyms for Continuous and for And et cetera.
We could create a simp set that is used to preprocess the goal, including the lemmas true_and and and_true?

Maybe the example was too simple. That's not the problem. The problem is that you need to, based solely on the structure of the resulting predicate (because this is the only information you have after typeclass search succeeds), determine which pieces of it come from CanLift predicates so that you can enumerate all the options.

Let's take the example of lifting ι → E →ₗ[𝕜] F to ι → E →L[𝕜] F. If we want maximal usability in the outParam approach, we need the lifting condition for linear maps to be Continuous, which would make the lifting condition for this parametric lift fun f ↦ ∀ i, Continuous (f i). From that predicate, how do we know to tell the user that (at least when E is finite dimensional) an alternate option is ∀ i, True?
We could add to our simp set the lemma that linear maps are continuous under some type class assumption?
